screens.title: Advanced Networking: Decode JSON & Send POSTs
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to turn raw bytes from the network into useful Swift objects and how to send structured data back to a server. We'll focus on the two core tools in the Foundation networking stack: JSONDecoder for deserializing JSON Data into your Codable types, and JSONEncoder with URLRequest to perform POST requests. You will see how to encode a Post object, set the Content-Type header so the server can parse your payload, and handle failures at three levels: network connectivity, HTTP response status codes, and decoding errors. A practical example will walk through creating a new Post, sending it, and decoding the server's response. That pattern — encode, set headers, send, check status, decode — is the workflow you will reuse across APIs. By the end you'll be able to make your app both a consumer and a creator of A P I resources, and you'll know what common mistakes to avoid when decoding or submitting JSON. Ready to explore decoding strategies, request construction, and robust error handling?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Advanced Networking

Decode JSON responses into Codable types, compose POST requests with JSONEncoder, and handle errors across network, HTTP, and decoding stages.

In this lesson
JSON decoding fundamentals

Why JSONDecoder and Codable models are essential for structured data.

Coming up
POST requests

How to encode a Swift object and assign it to httpBody with proper headers.

Why it matters
Reliable client-server flow

Work with APIs safely by checking status codes and decoding responses reliably.

Explore Key Topics
Decode JSON
Use JSONDecoder with Decodable types; configure date and key strategies to match the API.
Compose POST
Encode Codable objects with JSONEncoder into the httpBody and set Content-Type to application/json.
Handle errors
Differentiate network errors, HTTP status failures, and decoding exceptions for clear user feedback.
Visual Concept
Encode → Send → Check → Decode
1. Encode a Codable Swift object to JSON Data.
2. Create URLRequest, set httpMethod to POST, set Content-Type header, and assign httpBody.
3. Send request, inspect network error and HTTP status code.
4. Decode returned Data into your Codable response model.
Tip: Log the JSON string for debugging, but rely on Codable for production parsing.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

First, you will master using JSONDecoder to parse Data into Codable or Decodable Swift types, which makes server responses usable objects in your code. For example, decoding an array of Post objects lets your UI display titles and bodies without string parsing. Second, you will construct URLRequest objects for POST operations, ensuring the httpMethod is set to POST and the request is valid. Third, you will learn to encode a Codable Swift object using JSONEncoder and place the resulting JSON Data into httpBody while setting Content-Type to application/json. That step is what turns a local model into a network payload the server can parse. Fourth, you will implement comprehensive error handling that distinguishes network connectivity failures, HTTP status code problems, and JSON decoding errors so your app can present actionable messages. Each objective is practical: you will practice by encoding a Post, sending it, and decoding the server response. These skills let you build features like creating posts, submitting forms, and syncing state with an A P I.

screens.title: JSONDecoder and Decoding Data
screens.narratorSegment: JSONDecoder is the standard Foundation tool for converting JSON Data into Swift types that conform to Decodable or Codable. The decoder reads bytes and maps JSON keys to your model's properties, turning raw network responses into typed values you can use safely. A common pattern is to make a Post struct conform to Codable, then call decoder. decode(Post. self, from: data) inside a do-catch. Always wrap decoding in do-catch because the operation can throw when keys are missing, types mismatch, or the JSON is malformed. For example, if the server sends an array, decode([Post]. self, from: data). JSONDecoder is configurable: set dateDecodingStrategy when dates arrive as strings or timestamps, and set keyDecodingStrategy to convert snake_case keys to camelCase properties without custom CodingKeys. A frequent misconception is treating JSON as a String; printing JSON is useful for debugging, but it is brittle to parse strings manually. The concrete benefit here is type safety—after decoding, you can access post. title and post. body directly with compiler checks. As a takeaway, remember: decoding fails for structural mismatches; inspect the thrown error and compare your model to the server payload. Can you identify when to use decode(_:from:) for an array versus a single object?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › JSONDecoder
Definition

JSONDecoder

A decoder that maps JSON Data to your Decodable or Codable Swift types. Use do-catch to surface and handle decoding errors.

Common configurations
  • dateDecodingStrategy to parse server date formats.
  • keyDecodingStrategy to convert snake_case to camelCase automatically.
  • Decode an array with decode([Post].self, from: data) when the payload is an array.
Key Takeaway

Decoding gives typed models and prevents fragile string parsing; configure strategies to match the API shape.

Code example
let decoder = JSONDecoder()
// Example: convert snake_case to camelCase
// decoder.keyDecodingStrategy = .convertFromSnakeCase

do {
  let post = try decoder.decode(Post.self, from: data)
  // Use post.title and post.body safely
} catch {
  // Inspect error to determine mismatch
}
Concrete example

If you receive {"user_id":1,"title":"Hi"}, use keyDecodingStrategy or CodingKeys to map user_id to userId. Missing this mapping causes keyNotFound errors.

Misconception: printing JSON as a String is enough. It helps debugging, but typed decoding is necessary for stable code and compile-time safety.

screens.title: Designing Codable Models
screens.narratorSegment: Codable models are the bridge between JSON and typed Swift code. A struct like Post that conforms to Codable establishes the keys and types the decoder and encoder expect. When building these structs, give optional properties where the server might omit fields, such as id when creating a new resource. The chapter example uses id as Int? to indicate it can be nil during creation and filled by the server on response. Use custom CodingKeys when JSON names diverge from Swift property names, or use keyDecodingStrategy for common patterns like snake_case. A common source of decoding errors is a structural mismatch: you expected a String but received a number, or a key is absent. Another frequent mistake is not making fields optional when the A P I sometimes omits them. For encoding, ensure values you send match server expectations and that computed properties are not included unless intended. The practical benefit is clarity: your UI and networking code work against documented, predictable types rather than ad-hoc dictionaries. To test, compare a printed JSON string to your model and adjust optionality or keys until decoding succeeds consistently. Where might you prefer keyDecodingStrategy over custom CodingKeys? Consider consistency and small A P I shape changes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Codable Models
Definition

Codable Model Best Practices

  • Use Int? for server-assigned IDs that are nil at creation.
  • Make fields optional if the API can omit them.
  • Use CodingKeys or keyDecodingStrategy to resolve naming differences.
Common mistake

Treat every JSON field as required. Missing keys cause decoding errors unless marked optional.

Example Post struct
struct Post: Codable, Identifiable {
  let id: Int? // nil when creating a new post
  let userId: Int
  var title: String
  var body: String
}
Scenario

When creating a post, id is nil locally. After POST, server returns a created post with an id. Make id optional to avoid decoding errors before creation.

screens.title: Constructing a POST Request
screens.narratorSegment: Sending data to a server uses POST requests that carry the payload in the request body. The process is systematic: first initialize a URL with your endpoint and create a URLRequest(url:). Then set request. httpMethod to "POST". Next, convert your Codable model to JSON Data using JSONEncoder and assign that Data to request. httpBody. Crucially, set the Content-Type header to application/json with request. setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type") so the server interprets the body correctly. If the A P I requires authentication, set an Authorization header as well. A common mistake is to forget to set httpMethod or to set it to GET; that sends parameters via the URL and not the body. Another mistake is not setting Content-Type, which can cause the server to reject or misinterpret the payload. For debugging, you can pretty-print the JSON produced by JSONEncoder to the console, but avoid shipping prettyPrinted formatting in production unless needed. Remember to handle encoding errors from JSONEncoder using do-catch and to propagate meaningful error messages to the UI. Can you see why headers and method matter as much as the body when interacting with APIs?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › POST Construction
Process

Build a POST request

  1. Create a URL and URLRequest(url:).
  2. Set request.httpMethod = "POST".
  3. Encode your Codable object with JSONEncoder.
  4. Assign encoded Data to request.httpBody.
  5. Set headers like Content-Type and Authorization as needed.
Common mistake

Using GET or leaving out Content-Type leads to server misinterpretation or rejection of the JSON body.

Compact code pattern
var request = URLRequest(url: apiURL)
request.httpMethod = "POST"
request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
let jsonData = try JSONEncoder().encode(post)
request.httpBody = jsonData
// then URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: request) ...
Scenario: When sending a new post, userId and title must match server expectations. Forgetting Content-Type often causes a 400 response because the server cannot parse the body.

screens.title: Encoding with JSONEncoder and httpBody
screens.narratorSegment: JSONEncoder converts a Codable Swift object into Data suitable for assignment to a URLRequest's httpBody. Use JSONEncoder(). encode(post) inside a do-catch because encoding may throw when values cannot be represented. The chapter demonstrates setting encoder. outputFormatting =. prettyPrinted for readable logs, which helps when debugging server payloads. However, pretty printing increases payload size and is not necessary in production. After encoding, convert Data to String for a console print if you need to inspect the JSON structure. Next assign the Data to request. httpBody and set the Content-Type header. A concrete example: create a Post with id nil and userId set, encode it, set the httpBody, and submit. A common misconception is that encoding always succeeds; encoding can fail if your model contains types that don't map to JSON. You should catch and present an encoding error to the user or log it for developers. As a practical exercise, try encoding a Post with missing required fields and see the thrown error; then make those fields optional if the A P I omits them. What difference does prettyPrinted output make for debugging and network behavior?

keyIdea.title: Encode Safely
keyIdea.text: Use JSONEncoder in do-catch, optionally pretty-print for logs, and always assign the produced Data to httpBody with Content-Type set.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › JSONEncoder
Encoder Pattern

Encode a Post to Data

do {
  let encoder = JSONEncoder()
  encoder.outputFormatting = .prettyPrinted // helpful for logs
  let jsonData = try encoder.encode(newPost)
  request.httpBody = jsonData
} catch {
  // Handle encoding error and inform user
}
Tip: Convert jsonData to String to inspect the exact payload sent to the server for quick debugging.
Example output for debugging
{
  "userId": 1,
  "title": "My First Cohortia Post",
  "body": "This is a test post from my iOS app!"
}
Misconception check

Pretty printing is for logs and should not be relied on to change server parsing. Always set Content-Type so the server knows the data is JSON, regardless of formatting.

screens.title: Errors: Network vs HTTP vs Decoding
screens.narratorSegment: Network operations can fail in three distinct ways and each should be handled explicitly. First, network errors are captured as an Error? in the URLSession completion handler; these often map to URLError and represent connectivity problems like no internet or a timeout. For these, tell the user to check their connection and optionally retry. Second, HTTP status codes indicate how the server processed the request; cast URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and inspect statusCode. Codes outside 200–299, such as 401 Unauthorized or 500 Internal Server Error, are not decoding errors and should be surfaced with actionable messages, for example prompting for credentials on a 401. Third, decoding errors occur when Data arrives but JSONDecoder cannot map it to your model; this indicates a schema mismatch or malformed JSON and should be logged with the server payload for debugging. A common pitfall is conflating a decoding failure with a network problem; they have different fixes. For example, a 201 Created response with a malformed JSON body will still be an HTTP success but will throw during decoding. As a takeaway, design your completion handler to first check the Error, then the HTTP status, then attempt decoding in a do-catch. Which user message best fits each failure mode?

keyIdea.text: Handle network Error first, then check HTTP status codes, and finally handle JSONDecoder errors so each problem yields the correct user guidance.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Error Handling
Compare failure types
Network Error

Connectivity problems and timeouts captured as Error?; suggest retry or check connection.

HTTP Status

Non-2xx status codes indicate server-level issues; handle 401, 403, 404, 500 with specific user messages.

Decoding Error

Occurs when JSONDecoder cannot map Data to your model; log payload and compare model shape to JSON.

Actionable pattern
// completion handler skeleton
if let error = error { /* network: show retry */; return }
guard let http = response as? HTTPURLResponse,
      (200...299).contains(http.statusCode) else { /* handle status code */; return }
guard let data = data else { /* no data */; return }
// then decode in do-catch
Misconception: treating any non-success as decoding error. Instead, inspect the status code first because a 4xx or 5xx response means the request itself failed.

screens.title: Headers and Authorization
screens.narratorSegment: HTTP headers supply metadata about requests and responses. For JSON POSTs, the Content-Type header must be set to application/json so the server knows how to parse the body. Set it using request. setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type"). For authenticated APIs, include an Authorization header with a bearer token or A P I key, such as request. setValue("Bearer ", forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization"). Headers are strings; ensure tokens are kept secure and not logged in production. A common error is to place JSON payload in httpBody without setting Content-Type, which leads servers to reject or misinterpret the payload. Another issue is setting headers on a URL instead of the URLRequest—headers belong on the request object. Architecturally, consider centralizing request creation so headers and authentication are applied consistently across endpoints. For example, a simple request factory can attach Content-Type and Authorization automatically. Finally, remember to remove or refresh expired tokens based on server responses like 401. How will your app refresh tokens when the server reports unauthorized access? Headers and Authorization means always set content-type for json bodies and attach authorization headers when required; centralize header application to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, use http headers to describe content and pass credentials.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › HTTP Headers
Definition

Essential headers for JSON POSTs

  • Content-Type: application/json — tells the server how to parse httpBody.
  • Authorization: Bearer <token> — pass credentials for protected endpoints.
  • Other headers: Accept, custom API keys depending on the server contract.
Tip: centralize headers in a request builder so every request includes the same Content-Type and authorization behavior.
Code snippets
var request = URLRequest(url: apiURL)
request.httpMethod = "POST"
request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")
request.setValue("Bearer ", forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization")
// request.httpBody = jsonData
Misconception: storing tokens in plain text or logging them. Keep tokens secure and avoid printing them in logs for production builds.

screens.title: CreateNewPost: Full POST Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a complete POST function that sends a Post and decodes the created resource on success. Start by building a URL and URLRequest, then set httpMethod to POST and Content-Type to application/json. Use JSONEncoder to encode the Post into Data and assign it to httpBody. Launch a data task with URLSession. shared. dataTask(with: request). In the completion handler first check if an Error exists — this indicates a network-level failure. Next cast response to HTTPURLResponse and verify the statusCode is in 200–299; if not, create a server error with the code to inform the user. Then confirm data exists; if so, attempt JSONDecoder(). decode(Post. self, from: data) in a do-catch. On success pass the decoded createdPost to the completion; on failure return the decoding error so the caller can log or display it. The chapter's function uses Result in the completion to make success and failure explicit. A typical misconception is ignoring the response type and assuming data always decodes; always check status codes before decoding. How would you surface a 401 differently from a decoding error in the UI?

narration.text: Let's walk through a complete POST function that sends a Post and decodes the created resource on success. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › createNewPost()
Function walkthrough
func createNewPost(post: Post, completion: @escaping (Result<Post, Error>) -> Void) {
  var request = URLRequest(url: URL(string: createPostAPIURLString)!)
  request.httpMethod = "POST"
  request.setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type")

  do {
    let jsonData = try JSONEncoder().encode(post)
    request.httpBody = jsonData
  } catch {
    completion(.failure(error))
    return
  }

  URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: request) { data, response, error in
    if let error = error { completion(.failure(error)); return }
    guard let httpResponse = response as? HTTPURLResponse,
          (200...299).contains(httpResponse.statusCode) else {
      let code = (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode ?? -1
      completion(.failure(NSError(domain:"HTTPError", code: code, userInfo:nil)))
      return
    }
    guard let data = data else { completion(.failure(URLError(.zeroBytesInResource))); return }
    do {
      let decoder = JSONDecoder()
      let createdPost = try decoder.decode(Post.self, from: data)
      completion(.success(createdPost))
    } catch { completion(.failure(error)) }
  }.resume()
}
Concrete example: sending a Post with userId 1. If server returns 201 and a JSON post with an ID, decoding succeeds and you can display the created post details in the UI.

screens.title: Fetching and Decoding a GET Response
screens.narratorSegment: Decoding applies equally to GET requests; when you fetch a resource the pattern is similar but without encoding a body. Create a URL, call URLSession. shared. dataTask(with: url) and in the completion handler handle error, check HTTP status codes, then decode the returned Data with JSONDecoder. For example, fetchPostAPIURLString in the chapter shows fetching a single Post, checking a 2xx status, and decoding Post. self. Always guard that data exists before decoding. A common mistake is decoding before checking the status code; the server may return an error page with H T M L or a different JSON schema which causes decoding to fail. Use the same do-catch approach to surface decoding errors and log the raw Data for debugging. Also consider decoupling network logic from UI by returning a Result type or using an ObservableObject that publishes loading state, the decoded model, and errorMessage. In short, GET responses require the same layered checks and the same careful comparison between model and payload. What logging or safeguards will you add when you see unexpected decoding failures? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to turn raw bytes from the network into useful Swift objects and how to send structured data back to a server. We'll focus on the two core tools in the Foundation networking stack: JSONDecoder for deserializing JSON Data into your Codable types, and JSONEncoder with URLRequest to perform POST requests. You will see how to encode a Post object, set the Content-Type header so the server can parse your payload, and handle failures at three levels: network connectivity, HTTP response status codes, and decoding errors. A practical example will walk through creating a new Post, sending it, and decoding the server's response. That pattern — encode, set headers, send, check status, decode — is the workflow you will reuse across APIs. By the end you'll be able to make your app both a consumer and a creator of A P I resources, and you'll know what common mistakes to avoid when decoding or submitting JSON. Ready to explore decoding strategies, request construction, and robust error handling?

Over the next screens you'll develop four concrete skills that let your app both read and write JSON safely. First, you will master using JSONDecoder to parse Data into Codable or Decodable Swift types, which makes server responses usable objects in your code. For example, decoding an array of Post objects lets your UI display titles and bodies without string parsing. Second, you will construct URLRequest objects for POST operations, ensuring the httpMethod is set to POST and the request is valid. Third, you will learn to encode a Codable Swift object using JSONEncoder and place the resulting JSON Data into httpBody while setting Content-Type to application/json. That step is what turns a local model into a network payload the server can parse. Fourth, you will implement comprehensive error handling that distinguishes network connectivity failures, HTTP status code problems, and JSON decoding errors so your app can present actionable messages. Each objective is practical: you will practice by encoding a Post, sending it, and decoding the server response. These skills let you build features like creating posts, submitting forms, and syncing state with an A P I.

This second objectives slide connects each target to a practical practice you will perform. For JSONDecoder, you will decode a server payload into a Post struct and update UI state. For building POST URLRequests, you will construct a request with the target URL and set httpMethod to POST, which is essential because GET would send parameters on the URL instead of the body. For encoding, you'll use JSONEncoder to make Data from a Post object and assign it to httpBody, then set the Content-Type header so the server reads the body as JSON. For error handling, you will implement completion handlers that inspect an Error first, then cast URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse to inspect statusCode, and finally attempt decoding inside a do-catch. Practically, you will create a PostCreator observable that publishes loading state, createdPost, and errorMessage so the UI can show progress and results. Each practice step maps to a verified milestone: sending a post and showing the created post or an explicit error message.

JSONDecoder is the standard Foundation tool for converting JSON Data into Swift types that conform to Decodable or Codable. The decoder reads bytes and maps JSON keys to your model's properties, turning raw network responses into typed values you can use safely. A common pattern is to make a Post struct conform to Codable, then call decoder. decode(Post. self, from: data) inside a do-catch. Always wrap decoding in do-catch because the operation can throw when keys are missing, types mismatch, or the JSON is malformed. For example, if the server sends an array, decode([Post]. self, from: data). JSONDecoder is configurable: set dateDecodingStrategy when dates arrive as strings or timestamps, and set keyDecodingStrategy to convert snake_case keys to camelCase properties without custom CodingKeys. A frequent misconception is treating JSON as a String; printing JSON is useful for debugging, but it is brittle to parse strings manually. The concrete benefit here is type safety—after decoding, you can access post. title and post. body directly with compiler checks. As a takeaway, remember: decoding fails for structural mismatches; inspect the thrown error and compare your model to the server payload. Can you identify when to use decode(_:from:) for an array versus a single object?

Codable models are the bridge between JSON and typed Swift code. A struct like Post that conforms to Codable establishes the keys and types the decoder and encoder expect. When building these structs, give optional properties where the server might omit fields, such as id when creating a new resource. The chapter example uses id as Int? to indicate it can be nil during creation and filled by the server on response. Use custom CodingKeys when JSON names diverge from Swift property names, or use keyDecodingStrategy for common patterns like snake_case. A common source of decoding errors is a structural mismatch: you expected a String but received a number, or a key is absent. Another frequent mistake is not making fields optional when the A P I sometimes omits them. For encoding, ensure values you send match server expectations and that computed properties are not included unless intended. The practical benefit is clarity: your UI and networking code work against documented, predictable types rather than ad-hoc dictionaries. To test, compare a printed JSON string to your model and adjust optionality or keys until decoding succeeds consistently. Where might you prefer keyDecodingStrategy over custom CodingKeys? Consider consistency and small A P I shape changes.

Sending data to a server uses POST requests that carry the payload in the request body. The process is systematic: first initialize a URL with your endpoint and create a URLRequest(url:). Then set request. httpMethod to "POST". Next, convert your Codable model to JSON Data using JSONEncoder and assign that Data to request. httpBody. Crucially, set the Content-Type header to application/json with request. setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type") so the server interprets the body correctly. If the A P I requires authentication, set an Authorization header as well. A common mistake is to forget to set httpMethod or to set it to GET; that sends parameters via the URL and not the body. Another mistake is not setting Content-Type, which can cause the server to reject or misinterpret the payload. For debugging, you can pretty-print the JSON produced by JSONEncoder to the console, but avoid shipping prettyPrinted formatting in production unless needed. Remember to handle encoding errors from JSONEncoder using do-catch and to propagate meaningful error messages to the UI. Can you see why headers and method matter as much as the body when interacting with APIs?

JSONEncoder converts a Codable Swift object into Data suitable for assignment to a URLRequest's httpBody. Use JSONEncoder(). encode(post) inside a do-catch because encoding may throw when values cannot be represented. The chapter demonstrates setting encoder. outputFormatting =. prettyPrinted for readable logs, which helps when debugging server payloads. However, pretty printing increases payload size and is not necessary in production. After encoding, convert Data to String for a console print if you need to inspect the JSON structure. Next assign the Data to request. httpBody and set the Content-Type header. A concrete example: create a Post with id nil and userId set, encode it, set the httpBody, and submit. A common misconception is that encoding always succeeds; encoding can fail if your model contains types that don't map to JSON. You should catch and present an encoding error to the user or log it for developers. As a practical exercise, try encoding a Post with missing required fields and see the thrown error; then make those fields optional if the A P I omits them. What difference does prettyPrinted output make for debugging and network behavior?

Network operations can fail in three distinct ways and each should be handled explicitly. First, network errors are captured as an Error? in the URLSession completion handler; these often map to URLError and represent connectivity problems like no internet or a timeout. For these, tell the user to check their connection and optionally retry. Second, HTTP status codes indicate how the server processed the request; cast URLResponse to HTTPURLResponse and inspect statusCode. Codes outside 200–299, such as 401 Unauthorized or 500 Internal Server Error, are not decoding errors and should be surfaced with actionable messages, for example prompting for credentials on a 401. Third, decoding errors occur when Data arrives but JSONDecoder cannot map it to your model; this indicates a schema mismatch or malformed JSON and should be logged with the server payload for debugging. A common pitfall is conflating a decoding failure with a network problem; they have different fixes. For example, a 201 Created response with a malformed JSON body will still be an HTTP success but will throw during decoding. As a takeaway, design your completion handler to first check the Error, then the HTTP status, then attempt decoding in a do-catch. Which user message best fits each failure mode?

HTTP headers supply metadata about requests and responses. For JSON POSTs, the Content-Type header must be set to application/json so the server knows how to parse the body. Set it using request. setValue("application/json", forHTTPHeaderField: "Content-Type"). For authenticated APIs, include an Authorization header with a bearer token or A P I key, such as request. setValue("Bearer ", forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization"). Headers are strings; ensure tokens are kept secure and not logged in production. A common error is to place JSON payload in httpBody without setting Content-Type, which leads servers to reject or misinterpret the payload. Another issue is setting headers on a URL instead of the URLRequest—headers belong on the request object. Architecturally, consider centralizing request creation so headers and authentication are applied consistently across endpoints. For example, a simple request factory can attach Content-Type and Authorization automatically. Finally, remember to remove or refresh expired tokens based on server responses like 401. How will your app refresh tokens when the server reports unauthorized access? Headers and Authorization means always set content-type for json bodies and attach authorization headers when required; centralize header application to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, use http headers to describe content and pass credentials.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
